text: A built image can sit on your machine, or get pushed to a registry — a server that stores images, organized into named repositories, each with one or more tagged versions. Docker Hub is the default; AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, and GitHub each run their own too.

Every image reference follows the same shape: an optional registry host, a namespace, a repository, and a tag. Leave the host off and Docker assumes Docker Hub. And latest isn't a special keyword — it's just whatever was last pushed without an explicit version, which is exactly why it's a bad choice for anything you actually want to reproduce later.

Before you can push anything, a repository has to exist to receive it. On Docker Hub that's a short form — a name, and a choice between public and private. Public means searchable and pullable by anyone; private restricts it to your account.

Three commands move it over. Login authenticates once. Tag doesn't copy anything — it adds a second, registry-shaped name to the same local image. And push is what actually uploads the layers — layers already sitting in the registry from a previous push get skipped.
A registry isn't just where you push to, either — it's where official, maintained base images live too, searchable right on Docker Hub's own browse pages, compliance details and all.
And you don't even have to leave Docker Desktop to browse one. Registry Explorer sits in the same sidebar as Containers, Images, and Builds — a registry is just one more thing this app manages.
Tag, then push — and the image is reproducible anywhere that can pull it. That's Chapter One. Chapter Two starts packaging an actual AI application into one of these.
